story_text.value:
We've been working on a small tool that can help with huge (or really, any size) Gmail inboxes. It's meant for people who have let their inbox grow for years and don't know where to start.

We had this idea after talking to a lot of people about how they use their email, and one thing that kept coming up was how hard it is to keep up when you receive a lot of emails. Things pile up and cleaning up starts to feel impossible.

One important detail: the tool never performs any destructive operations on your email. The most it can do to a message is archive it (move it to the All Mail folder), where it stays available for search, so you never lose any messages as a result.

It combines multiple approaches to inbox cleanup: - You choose a cutoff date to archive everything before that - With some help from OpenAI, we find other groups of emails you may want to archive - We detect newsletters you rarely open and let you unsubscribe in one click - For transactional emails you rarely open (e.g. tool notifications), we suggest filters that skip the inbox and keep them under a label instead

At the end, you can undo all the inbox changes you made.

Gmail API calls happen client-side. Also, your messages and contacts are not stored on our servers. Some message metadata and snippets are sent to OpenAI to help with categorization.

Curious how many of you actually use inbox zero, or have considered trying it?

Happy to get your feedback.

title.value: Show HN: Inbox Cleanup – get to inbox zero in Gmail

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Demetrius.

When OpenAI launched Dots (always-on agents in ChatGPT that run in the background, connect to your apps, and ask before risky actions), I wanted to set one up and went looking for examples of what other people were telling theirs. I couldn't find any.

Each Dot comes down to three things: its instructions, the apps it can reach, and Custom Rules (Allow / Require approval / Block). The rules matter most, because they decide what the agent does without asking you. They're also the part nobody was sharing.

So I built DotBotDirectory.

Each entry has the Dot's job, its instructions, its connected apps, and its three rule lists. One click copies the instructions and rules together so you can paste them into your own Dot.

Where it stands:

- 26 starter entries, written by me from ideas people published in early Dot write-ups. Each one credits its source.

- None of them have been tested on a real Dot yet, and they're labelled "Starter - untested". I'll mark entries as tested once someone confirms one works.

- Copy counts start at zero, so nothing looks more popular than it is.

- Free, and not affiliated with OpenAI.

Two questions for anyone who has run a Dot:

1. What did you put in Require approval vs Block? That's where I think most of the value is.

2. Did your Dot ever do something you didn't expect? I'd like to turn those cases into rules other people can copy.

Happy to answer anything.

story_text.value: There are project management platforms, which should make possible at the same time that you can let run a LLM of your own choice over all tickets, documents, conversations, meetings, emails and so on that have to do with a project. I know that there are already such systems and that somehow every third person is building on it. So far so good. I ask myself only where probably the development will go to. The users of course still access the frontend and operate it like you actually always operated it but for developers this often does not apply because they only move around in the cloud console. What do you mean how one will work with such systems in the future? Because also in future you will still work with other humans and maybe you do not want to offer your complete project contents to a provider like OpenAI, because they will surely also offers such systems. But the question is if you really want to throw everything in there and the question is if you really want it that all your data are at one of the big AI provider. If it is now Google, OpenAI or Anthropic.

story_text.value:
Built dotlink to give chatgpt codex abilities, letting chatgpt web, the new dots and spaces, build and run tools and access files directly in your local machine.

Been using it for a while, when I'm out of codex limits or giving chatgpt controlled access to several machines without installing chatgpt app. So thought I'll package it for others to use.

It’s a single statically linked lightweight Rust MCP binary with fine-grained read/write/shell permissions, profuiles and a Bubblewrap sandbox on Linux and also works without any local port (uses OpenAI MCP tunnel) or third-party relay.

Please check it out: https://github.com/abird-ai/dotlink

story_text.value:
Today we’re opening Datastory to everyone!

Datastory is a platform for turning data, your own or the world’s open data, into charts that people can understand and trust.

Please try it out and let us know what we can improve!

A little backstory I’ve spent my career trying to make data understandable and useful, from helping animate Hans Rosling's TED Talks at Gapminder to building data platforms for organizations in health, research, media and the public sector.

Every project taught me the same thing: organizations were building similar platforms from scratch, at great cost, and communicating data well remained slow, expensive, expert work.

That’s why we started Datastory as a non-profit, publishing data journalism and building our own tools because nothing else was fast enough. Over the years those tools became the product, and today they're used by public agencies, researchers and newsrooms.

Under the hood, the open data catalog sits on a knowledge graph built on linked data standards (RDF), with pipelines orchestrated in Dagster. Sources are joined semantically, and templates connect directly to the graph.

The free plan covers the full range of features, so you can try everything out. Tell us what’s missing or broken :) We’ll be here all day.

title.value: Show HN: Datastory, Data storytelling with AI and an open knowledge graph

story_text.value:
I kept thinking about how a lot of us have to be online to do our work each day. It is not uncommon to have other open tabs with social media, games, or whatever. Why not turn your current page, whatever site you are on, into a game?

So I built DOM-defense. Once you click play on the current tab and it overlays a tower-defense game on that page. The path snakes its way through the pages hyperlinks. You place towers in the empty space. Enemies march alont the path and if they break the last blockade, you lose. Survive 100 waves and you win.

A couple of details that mattered to me while building it:

Variety - Every page is a different map (news, docs, Wikipedia, whatever). You are not confined to set levels. Every site is different so it naturally creates infinite variety

Work within a users current flow - Instead of opening other tabs or another site, I wanted a user to not have to "go outside" of their normal workflow

Difficulty/Fun factor - I spent some time tuning it to make it difficult, but beatable. Finding the balance is difficult when a user can literally play it on any site

It’s free on the Chrome Web Store:

https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dom-defense/bglbhkd...

Curious what pages break it hardest, or what would make the loop more fun. Happy to answer any questions too.

title.value: Show HN: DOM-defense – turn your current webpage into a tower defense level
